Course Format and Materials

The assignments in this course come in many formats: audio, video, and reading (primary sources, textbook excerpts, and historical scholarship).

All materials are available in a shared folder, linked on Canvas. Important: you can download the entire folder, but I will update it throughout the semester, so check it frequently.

A Partially Flipped Classroom

Some of the lecture in this course is pre-recorded, so that class time can go to what is best done together: discussion, interactive lecture, exercises, and evaluation.

The readings and recorded lectures are due before the class session they are associated with on the syllabus. With few exceptions, preparation (reading, listening, taking notes) is work you do on your own, outside class. The vast majority of graded work in this course, in both evaluation and engagement, consists of in-class assignments that rely on that preparation (see Grading Policies).

A Typical Cycle

Before class:

  1. Listen to the audio lecture, casually: on the bus, or while waiting in line for your latte. It sets the stage.
  2. Watch the video lecture, actively, and take notes. This is where I lay out what you truly need to know to make sense of the readings.
  3. Do the readings.

In class:

  1. A quick quiz. Low-stress and low-consequence, for engagement points. If you did the reading and listened carefully, it should be easy.
  2. Interactive lecture. I revisit some of the same material, but this time I expect you to participate.
  3. Exercises and evaluation, which take up more than half of a typical class session.

AI can be a useful study aid while you prepare, if you use it well (see AI in This Course).

Pre-Recorded Audio Lectures

I use audio lectures to get across general ideas and big thematic points. Any important details you might want to take notes on, I save for the video lectures.

Low-key is not the same as optional, though. The audio lectures are required, and their content is fair game on quizzes.

Pre-Recorded Video Lectures

The video lectures are the workhorses of the course. They include visuals, and they carry the details worth taking notes on. The readings for a given session come from many different places (primary sources, textbook excerpts, historical scholarship), and the video lecture is what knits them together.

The quizzes at the start of class, which count toward engagement, draw on the recorded lectures.

Readings

Most class sessions have assigned primary sources, and some also have secondary overviews (for example, textbook excerpts or historical scholarship).

The primary sources are especially important: expect to reference them directly in oral and written in-class exercises. For how to cite them in writing, see the Writing Guidelines. Questions about a reading? Bring them to office hours.

Note-Taking

Developing your own, personalized note-taking system is an essential skill for your academic career. How you take notes will vary widely from person to person. That is fine, and expected.

From time to time, I will offer engagement points for evidence that you have put thought into your note-taking and are actively maintaining your notes. In other words, I may ask to see them in class.

For more on approaches to note-taking, see Note-Taking.

What to Bring

  • A pen (dark ink scans best)
  • A blank spiral notebook of your choice
  • A smartphone with a scanning app, installed in advance: Adobe Scan (Android / iPhone) or a similar app for quickly producing PDFs. The Notes app on iPhone and the Google Drive app on Android also have built-in document scanners.

Many assignments will ask you to write by hand in your notebook, scan the pages to a PDF, and upload the PDF to Canvas. The scan is your submission; the notebook itself stays with you. Unless instructed otherwise, upload your scan before you leave class. If you have a technical problem (dead battery, app trouble), hand me the page and I will scan it.

For other rules about phones, laptops, and recording in class, see Devices in Class.
